name: AI for Career Transition and Employment
objectives: Given your stage of transition, identify free official sources of job help and choose one to contact, with a contact method or appointment written down
Given one real job posting, list its must-haves, nice-to-haves and keywords with AI help and match them to your skills, with at least 10 keywords from the posting
Using your keyword list, write a one-page civilian résumé tailored to the posting with AI help, with at least five bullets in civilian words and numbers, every claim true and no private numbers
For the same job, write a short cover letter and an online profile summary with AI help, edited so they sound like you

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Free official transition and job help
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name three free official sources of job help and choose one to contact.
This lesson builds toward: Given your stage of transition, you will identify free official sources of job help and choose one to contact, with a contact method or appointment written down.
You do not have to do this alone. The Transition Assistance Program (TAP) is run by several agencies, including the Department of Labor, the Department of Defense and the VA. The Department of Labor's part includes employment workshops and one-on-one help through its Employment Navigator and Partnership Program at select installations. Find class schedules through your installation's transition office.
After you leave, American Job Centers (nearly 2,400 nationwide, found through CareerOneStop) help with job searches and training, and veterans get priority of service. The VA's Personalized Career Planning and Guidance program gives free career and education counseling, including résumé help, to eligible veterans and service members.
AI is a great writing partner, but a trained counselor knows your local job market and your benefits. Use both.
Step by step:
- Still serving: contact your installation's transition office about TAP.
- Out of service: find your nearest American Job Center on CareerOneStop.
- Read the VA's Personalized Career Planning and Guidance page and check eligibility.
- Book one appointment this week.
Words to know:
- TAP: Transition Assistance Program: training and help for service members moving to civilian life.
- American Job Center: a free Department of Labor-funded center for job search and training help.
- Priority of service: veterans are served first for many Department of Labor job and training programs.
Official sources:
- U.S. Department of Labor: Transition Assistance Program
- U.S. Department of Labor VETS: Find a job
- VA: Personalized Career Planning and Guidance
Try it now: Pick the one official source from this lesson that fits you now. Find its page or nearest office and write down how to contact it. Book or plan one appointment.
You can now name free official sources of job help and choose the right one to contact.

check.q: Which of these is a free official source of job help for transitioning service members?
options: A paid résumé site from an ad
TAP at your installation's transition office
check.why: TAP is the official, free transition program for service members.

check.q: You have used AI to draft your résumé. What else do you do?
options: Ask a TAP, American Job Center or VA counselor to review it
Send it to every job without reading it
Skip counselors because AI is enough
Post it publicly with your phone number
check.why: AI helps you write, but a counselor knows local jobs and benefits and can catch mistakes.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Reading a job posting like a hiring manager
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pull the key requirements and keywords out of a job posting with AI help.
This lesson builds toward: Given one real job posting, you will list its must-haves, nice-to-haves and keywords with AI help and match them to your skills, with at least 10 keywords from the posting.
Every job posting tells you what the employer wants to hear. Many companies use an applicant tracking system (ATS) that scans résumés for words that match the posting, so using the posting's own words matters.
Copy a real posting into an AI assistant and ask: "List the must-have requirements, the nice-to-have skills, and the 10 most important keywords from this posting. Then tell me which of my skills match: I was a Marine Corps supply chief for 7 years, led 10 Marines, managed $2 million in equipment."
Check the AI's list against the posting yourself. If you meet most of the must-haves, apply. Many people apply without meeting every nice-to-have.
Step by step:
- Choose one real job posting.
- Paste the posting (not your private details) into an AI assistant.
- Ask for must-haves, nice-to-haves and top keywords.
- Ask which of your skills match.
- Check the list against the posting yourself.
Words to know:
- Applicant tracking system (ATS): software employers use to collect and scan résumés for matching words.
- Keyword: an important word or phrase from the posting, like "inventory control".
- Must-have: a requirement you need to be considered.
Try it now: Find one real job posting you would want. Ask an AI assistant to list its must-haves, nice-to-haves and top 10 keywords, and which of your skills match.
You can now pull the requirements and keywords out of a job posting and match them to your experience.

check.q: What is a nice-to-have in a job posting?
options: A requirement you must meet to apply
A skill that helps but is not required
check.why: Nice-to-haves are extras; you can still apply if you meet most must-haves.

check.q: You paste a job posting into an AI. What do you ask for?
options: "List the must-haves, nice-to-haves and top 10 keywords, and which of my skills match."
"Write my Social Security number on it."
check.why: A clear request pulls out the requirements and keywords you need to tailor your résumé.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing a tailored civilian résumé
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft a one-page résumé tailored to one posting, with civilian words and numbers.
This lesson builds toward: Using your keyword list, you will write a one-page civilian résumé tailored to the posting with AI help, with at least five bullets in civilian words and numbers, every claim true and no private numbers.
A civilian résumé is usually one or two pages, not a full service record. It has a short summary at the top, your experience with bullets, your skills, your education and certifications. Use civilian job titles where they fit ("supply chain supervisor" rather than "supply chief") and explain what you did, how big it was, and the result.
Give the AI your experience in plain words and the keywords from Lesson 2: "Write a one-page résumé for this logistics coordinator posting. Use these keywords. My experience: [plain description]. Use strong verbs and numbers, no military acronyms."
Leave out your Social Security number, DD-214 details, full birth date and security clearance details beyond what the posting asks for. Never let AI add things you did not do. Then ask a TAP, American Job Center or VA counselor to look at it.
Step by step:
- Write your experience in plain words: what, how big, what result.
- Give AI the keywords from the posting.
- Ask for a one-page résumé with a summary, experience bullets and skills.
- Replace military terms and check every claim is true.
- Remove private details and ask a counselor to review it.
Words to know:
- Summary: two or three lines at the top of a résumé saying who you are and what you offer.
- Tailor: change your résumé to match one specific job.
Try it now: Use your keyword list from Lesson 2. Ask an AI assistant to draft a one-page résumé for that posting. Change any line that is not exactly true.
You can now write a one-page civilian résumé tailored to a specific job posting with AI help.

check.q: Why does a tailored résumé use the posting's own words?
options: So scanning software and the hiring manager see the match
So you can skip the cover letter
check.why: Applicant tracking systems and hiring managers look for the posting's keywords.

check.q: The AI's draft says you earned a certification you do not have. What do you do?
options: Say you are earning it soon
Remove it so every claim is true
check.why: Every claim on your résumé must be true.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing a short cover letter and profile summary
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to write a short cover letter and an online profile summary in your own voice.
This lesson builds toward: For the same job, you will write a short cover letter and an online profile summary with AI help, edited so they sound like you.
A cover letter is a short letter that says why you want this job and why you fit. Keep it to three short paragraphs: why this job, your two or three best matches with proof, and a polite close.
Ask the AI: "Write a 3-paragraph cover letter for this posting, using my résumé. Sound confident but not stiff, no military jargon." Then make it sound like you: change words you would never say.
An online profile summary, for example on LinkedIn, is two to four sentences about who you are and what work you want. Ask the AI for three versions, pick one and edit it.
Step by step:
- Give AI the posting and your résumé.
- Ask for a three-paragraph cover letter.
- Edit it so it sounds like you.
- Ask for three versions of a two-to-four-sentence profile summary.
- Pick one, edit it and use it.
Words to know:
- Cover letter: a short letter sent with a résumé saying why you want and fit the job.
- Profile summary: a few sentences about you at the top of an online career profile.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for a three-paragraph cover letter for the job from Lesson 2. Change at least three phrases so it sounds like you.
You can now write a short cover letter and a profile summary with AI help, in your own voice.

check.q: How long is a good cover letter?
check.why: Three short paragraphs cover why this job, your best matches and a polite close.

check.q: The AI's cover letter uses words you would never say. What do you do?
options: Change at least three phrases so it sounds like you
check.why: Your cover letter should sound like you, so the interview matches the letter.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Practicing interviews with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Practice a 60-second introduction and two STAR answers with an AI interviewer.
This lesson builds toward: With an AI acting as a hiring manager, you will practice a 60-second "tell me about yourself" answer and STAR answers out loud, at least twice, writing down one strength and one fix.
Most interviews start with "Tell me about yourself." A good answer takes about 60 seconds: who you are now, your most relevant experience, and why you want this job. Do not tell your whole service history.
For "Tell me about a time..." questions, use STAR: situation, task, action, result. Example: "Our unit's vehicle readiness was at 70% (situation). I was asked to raise it before an inspection (task). I set up a daily parts tracker and a two-shift schedule (action). Readiness hit 92% in six weeks (result)."
Ask the AI to act as an interviewer: "Act as a hiring manager for this job. Ask me one question at a time. After each answer, give me one thing I did well and one thing to improve." Practice out loud. If you use voice mode, speak naturally.
Step by step:
- Write a 60-second "tell me about yourself" answer.
- Write two STAR stories from your service.
- Ask AI to act as the interviewer, one question at a time.
- Answer out loud and ask for one strength and one fix each time.
- Practice until it feels natural.
Words to know:
- STAR: situation, task, action, result: a way to tell a short story about your work.
- Behavioral question: an interview question that asks about a time you did something.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to act as a hiring manager for your chosen job. Answer three questions out loud, including "Tell me about yourself", and write down the feedback.
You can now give a 60-second introduction and answer behavioral questions using STAR.

check.q: What does the A in a STAR answer stand for?
check.why: STAR is situation, task, action, result; the action is what you did.

check.q: You want to practice with an AI interviewer. Which request do you use?
options: "Ask one question at a time and give me one strength and one fix."
"Give me all the answers to memorize."
check.why: One question at a time with feedback lets you practice and improve each answer.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Searching smart and spotting job scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Search official job sources and spot the warning signs of a job scam.
This lesson builds toward: When you search for jobs, you will search official job sources and identify the warning signs of a job scam, paying nothing and sharing no private numbers before a real offer.
Search where real jobs are posted: company websites, the CareerOneStop Job Finder, American Job Centers, and for federal jobs USAJOBS and the Office of Personnel Management's FedsHireVets site, which explains federal hiring for veterans, including veterans' preference.
Scammers target job seekers. Warning signs: a job offer without an interview, a request to pay for training or equipment, a check to deposit and send money back, interviews only by text chat, or a request for your Social Security number or bank details before a real offer.
Ask an AI to point out warning signs in a suspicious posting, after removing your details. Then check the company yourself on its official website. Only give private details for real paperwork, after a real offer, through the employer's official process.
Step by step:
- Search company sites, CareerOneStop, American Job Centers and USAJOBS.
- Look for warning signs: no interview, upfront payment, check-and-send-back, text-only interviews.
- Do not give SSN or bank details before a real offer.
- Check the company on its official website.
- Ask AI to list warning signs in a suspicious posting.
Words to know:
- Veterans' preference: rules that give eligible veterans an advantage in federal hiring.
- Job scam: a fake job offer meant to steal money or personal information.
Official sources:
- U.S. Department of Labor VETS: Find a job
- Office of Personnel Management: FedsHireVets
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-page résumé tailored to your chosen posting and your 60-second "tell me about yourself" answer. Check every claim is true and there are no private numbers, then say the answer out loud twice.
You can now search official job sources, avoid job scams, and apply with a tailored résumé and a practiced introduction.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Tailored to the posting The résumé could be for any job; few of the posting's keywords appear. The résumé uses the posting's keywords and shows the must-haves the learner meets. The learner can point to where each must-have is shown. Civilian bullets with numbers Fewer than five bullets, or bullets with military slang and no numbers. At least five bullets in civilian words, with numbers or results, on one page. Every bullet shows what was done, how big it was and the result. True and private A claim is not true, or a Social Security, DD-214 or other private number appears. Every claim is true, and no private numbers appear. A counselor or trusted reader has checked it. 60-second answer The answer is much longer than 60 seconds or not about this job. About 60 seconds: who you are, relevant experience and why this job, said out loud twice. The learner used AI feedback to improve one part between the two tries. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Where are U.S. federal jobs posted?
check.why: USAJOBS is the official site for federal job postings.

check.q: A recruiter asks for your Social Security number before any interview. What do you do?
options: Send it so you do not lose the job
Do not send it; give it only for real paperwork after a real offer
check.why: Asking for private numbers before any interview or offer is a scam warning sign.
